title: Design Ordered Stream
description:
# Design Ordered Stream

A stream will receive exactly `n` pairs `(idKey, value)` in an arbitrary order. Each `idKey` is an integer from `1` to `n`, no two insertions use the same `idKey`, and each `value` is a lowercase string of length `5`.

Design `OrderedStream` so that after every insertion it returns the largest possible chunk of values that can now be emitted in increasing `idKey` order. If the current next id has not arrived yet, the returned chunk is empty even if larger ids are already buffered.

Implement the `OrderedStream` class:

* `OrderedStream(int n)` initializes the stream for ids `1` through `n`.
* `List<String> insert(int idKey, String value)` stores `(idKey, value)` and returns the newly available consecutive chunk starting at the smallest id that has not yet been returned.

The concatenation of all returned chunks must be exactly the values sorted by id. The stream must never return a value early and must never return the same id twice.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["OrderedStream", "insert", "insert", "insert", "insert", "insert"]
[[5], [3, "ccccc"], [1, "aaaaa"], [2, "bbbbb"], [5, "eeeee"], [4, "ddddd"]]

**Output:**
[null, [], ["aaaaa"], ["bbbbb", "ccccc"], [], ["ddddd", "eeeee"]]

**Explanation:**
The next id starts at `1`. Inserting id `3` cannot release anything because id `1` is still missing. Inserting id `1` releases `["aaaaa"]`. Inserting id `2` then releases ids `2` and `3` together. Id `5` waits until id `4` arrives, after which ids `4` and `5` are released together.

## Constraints

* `1 <= n <= 1000`
* `1 <= idKey <= n`
* `value.length == 5`
* `value` consists only of lowercase letters.
* Each call to `insert` has a unique `idKey`.
* Exactly `n` calls will be made to `insert`.

examples.explanation: Id 3 waits for id 1. Id 2 releases both ids 2 and 3. Id 5 waits until id 4 arrives.

solutions.name: Array with Release Pointer
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) total over all insert calls
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store each value at `values[idKey]` and keep `ptr` as the smallest id that has not been emitted yet. After every insertion, scan forward from `ptr` while the next slot is already filled, appending those values to the returned chunk.

## Key Insight
The pointer only moves to the right, so each id is inspected and emitted at most once across the whole stream. Out-of-order arrivals can wait in the array until the missing prefix id appears.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n) total over all insert calls, O(k) for a call that emits k values
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: HashMap Sparse Buffer with Pointer
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) total expected over all insert calls
solutions.description:
## Approach
Keep a `HashMap` from id to value for arrived entries. The same `ptr` marks the next id that should be released; after inserting, repeatedly check whether the map contains `ptr`, remove it, and advance.

## Key Insight
This route separates the ordering rule from the storage shape. The stream is correct because only `ptr` decides what can be emitted, while the map is just a sparse waiting room for out-of-order ids.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n) total expected over all insert calls
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: BitSet Readiness Table
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n) total over all insert calls
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store values in an array and store arrival state separately in a `BitSet`. On insertion, write the value, mark the id as ready, then emit the consecutive ready interval beginning at `ptr`.

## Key Insight
A separate readiness table avoids relying on `null` as the only sentinel. That pattern is useful when stored values could have a special empty representation or when the value array should not be used as the presence flag.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n) total over all insert calls
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: TreeMap Ordered Pending Entries
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per insert plus emitted chunk size
solutions.description:
## Approach
Put arrived but not-yet-emitted ids in a `TreeMap`. The map keeps buffered ids ordered, so after each insertion inspect `firstEntry()` and release only while the smallest pending id is exactly `ptr`.

## Key Insight
The ordered map is useful because the smallest buffered id exposes the current blocking gap. If the smallest pending id is larger than `ptr`, no later id can be emitted; if it equals `ptr`, `pollFirstEntry()` releases the next value and advances the pointer.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) per inserted id and O(log n) per emitted id
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Min-Heap Buffered Ids
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per insert plus emitted chunk size
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store values by id in an array and push every arrived id into a min-heap. After each insertion, the heap top tells us the smallest buffered id; emit while that smallest id equals `ptr`.

## Key Insight
A min-heap is another way to express the same release rule. Larger ids may already be buffered, but the heap prevents them from hiding a missing smaller id because only the minimum ready id can be checked against `ptr`.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n) per insert and O(log n) for each emitted id
- Space Complexity: O(n)

tests.description: Canonical out-of-order stream releases chunks only when the current pointer is present.
Buffered higher ids are released only after the missing prefix id arrives.
Already ordered arrivals should return one value per insertion.
Reverse-order arrivals wait until id 1 arrives, then release the whole stream at once.
Single-entry streams release immediately and then finish.
A released prefix can be followed by later buffered suffix chunks.
Duplicate values must still be returned by id order, not by value identity.
Multiple gaps can close in stages while the pointer never moves backward.
